intermittent

in-ter-MIT-uhnt -- shares a root with 'transmit' and 'permit.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Intermittent is occurring at irregular intervals; not continuous or steady.

Intermittent power outages plagued the neighborhood throughout the storm.

Example

A dripping faucet doesn't run in one steady stream; its intermittent dripping comes every few minutes, pauses, then starts again, following no reliable pattern at all.

That on-and-off, irregular pattern with pauses in between is exactly what intermittent means. Unlike 'constant,' which never stops, intermittent starts and stops repeatedly.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fitful: Fitful describes activity that comes in restless, uneven bursts -- fitful sleep, a fitful breeze -- with an edge of agitation about it. Intermittent is the calmer, more technical word: something simply stops and starts at irregular intervals, with no suggestion of restlessness.

occasional: Occasional tells you something happens only now and then -- an occasional visit, an occasional treat -- and stresses how seldom it comes. Intermittent stresses the stop-start rhythm instead: the thing keeps cutting out and returning, however many times that happens.

patchy: Patchy means uneven in coverage or quality, with good stretches and bad ones side by side -- patchy fog, a patchy phone signal. Intermittent is about time rather than coverage: something switching off and on again at irregular, unpredictable intervals.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

constant: continuing without interruption

continuous: without any break or gap

Where it sits · how unpredictable the timing is — periodic → intermittent → sporadic

periodic vs. intermittent: Periodic can feel more predictable than intermittent -- periodic often suggests intervals that occur on a regular, expected schedule, while intermittent implies stopping and starting without any clear pattern.

sporadic vs. intermittent: Sporadic can feel even less predictable than intermittent: intermittent often describes something that pauses and resumes over a relatively short span, while sporadic suggests occurrences scattered unpredictably over a longer stretch of time.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — inter-

prefix — inter-: between (Latin)

root — -mittent

root — -mittent: to send, let go (Latin (mittere))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin intermittere meant 'to leave off' or 'interrupt,' built from inter- ('between') and mittere ('to send, let go'). Intermittent, at its root, describes something that lets go and then sends again, again and again -- the same root behind transmit.

Use the root in a new word: transmit

Use the root in a new word: transmit: The satellite was designed to transmit weather data back to Earth every few hours.
